definition.text: Models that describe and predict choices between separate alternatives, such as which mode of transport to take, rather than how much of something to buy.

facts.text: A model gives the probability that a person chooses a given alternative as a function of features of the alternatives and of the person.
They can be derived from utility theory, and only differences in utility between alternatives affect the choice probabilities.
The first applications were in transportation planning, and in market research the approach is commonly called conjoint analysis.
Common forms include binary logit and probit, multinomial and conditional logit, nested logit and mixed logit, usually estimated by maximum likelihood.
Standard logit assumes independence of irrelevant alternatives, a substitution pattern that is not always realistic; mixed logit relaxes it by allowing tastes to vary between people.

definition.text: A bias in contingent valuation where people struggle to put a value on one public good that is part of a larger set of similar goods.

facts.text: It suggests contingent valuation is not an unbiased way to measure policy effects in cost-benefit analysis.
Part-whole bias arises when willingness to pay for two policies valued separately does not add up to willingness to pay for both together.
Willingness to pay for a project is larger when it is asked about first than when it comes second in a sequence.
One fix asks first what people would pay for the whole set of items, then how much of that should go to the named item.
